Canada has no national workers' compensation system: each province and territory has its own
board or commission (WCB). The Association of Workers' Compensation Boards of Canada (AWCBC)
collects the claims they **accept** and publishes national statistics on **lost time claims**
(injuries and diseases that kept a worker off work) and **fatalities**. Read the module
[README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

*Source: AWCBC, National Work Injury/Disease Statistics Program (NWISP). The analyses and
interpretations in this notebook are those of the user, not of the AWCBC or its member boards.*

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.
- Parts marked *ENVH 460/560* are required for graduate students and optional for ENVH 312.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/ca-awcbc-nwisp/data/tidy")
read_tidy <- function(name) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name),
           col_types = cols(year = col_integer(), value = col_double(), .default = col_character()))
}

trend <- read_tidy("nwisp_jurisdiction_trend.csv")            # 1982 (claims) / 1993 (deaths) to 2024
by_province <- read_tidy("nwisp_jurisdiction.csv.gz")         # 2022-2024, by province
by_group <- read_tidy("nwisp_industry_occupation.csv.gz")     # 2023-2024, by industry or occupation

canada <- filter(by_province, jurisdiction == "Total")
```

# Part 1. Forty years of claims and deaths

```{r trend}
national <- trend |>
  filter(jurisdiction == "Total") |>
  select(outcome, year, value)

ggplot(national, aes(year, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Accepted claims, Canada", x = NULL, y = "Accepted claims")

national |>
  filter(year %in% c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2024)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = value)
```

**Questions**

1. By how much did lost time claims fall between 1990 and 2010? Did fatalities fall too?
2. Give two explanations for the fall in lost time claims other than safer workplaces (think about
   the economy, the kinds of jobs people do, and how compensation boards manage claims).
3. Why might fatalities not fall in the same way? (Hint: Part 3.)

# Part 2. Provinces and territories

```{r provinces, fig.height = 6}
trend |>
  filter(jurisdiction != "Total", outcome == "lost time claims", year >= 2010) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ jurisdiction, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Lost time claims by province or territory", x = NULL, y = "Accepted claims")

canada_by_year <- trend |>
  filter(outcome == "lost time claims", year >= 2021, jurisdiction != "Total") |>
  select(jurisdiction, year, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value)
canada_by_year
```

1. Which provinces have the most claims? Why can you not conclude that they are the most dangerous
   places to work? (There are no worker counts in this dataset.)

   whether these jumps reflect more injuries or changes in policy or reporting?

# Part 3. What kills workers in Canada?

Codes below 10 in the nature of injury classification are injuries; codes 10 and above are diseases.

```{r fatal-nature}
fatal_nature <- canada |>
  filter(outcome == "fatalities", characteristic == "nature of injury", code != "Total") |>
  mutate(type = if_else(suppressWarnings(as.integer(code)) < 10, "Injury", "Disease", missing = "Not coded"))

fatal_nature |>
  group_by(year, type) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(share = deaths / sum(deaths))

fatal_nature |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  arrange(desc(value)) |>
  select(code, category, deaths = value) |>
  head(8)
```

**Questions**

1. What share of accepted fatalities are from disease? Which diseases are most common?
2. Fatalities are counted in the year the claim is accepted. For a death from mesothelioma, how
   long ago might the exposure have been?
3. The US CFOI and Australian TIF modules count only deaths from injury. Compare the Canadian
   *injury* deaths with those counts. Why does the choice of definition matter for policy?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Industries

```{r industry}
industry <- canada |>
  filter(characteristic == "industry", year == 2024, code != "Total") |>
  select(outcome, category, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(desc(`lost time claims`))
industry

industry |>
  filter(category != "Not coded") |>
  ggplot(aes(`lost time claims`, fct_reorder(category, `lost time claims`))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Lost time claims by industry, Canada, 2024", x = "Accepted claims", y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which industries have the most lost time claims? The most fatalities? Why are the lists different?
2. Health care and social assistance has the most claims. Name three hazards in health care that
   lead to lost time.
3. How many fatalities have no industry coded? How does that limit what you can say?

# Part 5. Who is injured?

```{r gender-age}
canada |>
  filter(characteristic == "gender", code %in% c("1", "2"), year == 2024) |>
  select(outcome, category, value) |>
  group_by(outcome) |>
  mutate(share = value / sum(value))

canada |>
  filter(characteristic == "age", outcome == "fatalities", !code %in% c("Total", "12", "NC")) |>
  ggplot(aes(category, value, fill = factor(year))) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Accepted fatalities by age", x = NULL, y = "Fatalities", fill = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

**Questions**

1. Women make up almost half of lost time claims but a small share of fatalities. Why?
2. In which age group are fatalities most common? How does that relate to the disease deaths in Part 3?

# Part 6 (ENVH 460/560). Inside an industry

```{r inside-industry}
by_group |>
  filter(by == "industry", outcome == "lost time claims", characteristic == "event", year == 2024,
         group_code %in% c("23", "62"), code != "Total") |>
  group_by(group) |>
  slice_max(value, n = 5) |>
  select(group, category, value)

by_group |>
  filter(by == "occupation", outcome == "fatalities", characteristic == "nature of injury",
         year == 2024, code == "31") |>
  select(group, cancer_deaths = value) |>
  arrange(desc(cancer_deaths))
```

**Questions**

1. Compare the most common events in construction and in health care. What prevention
   priorities follow for each?
2. In health care, the most common event is "exposure to caustic, noxious, or allergenic
   substances". What kinds of exposures could be coded this way in a hospital or care home? How
   would you check?
3. Which occupation categories have the most accepted cancer deaths? The second category includes
   firefighters (NOC 43, front-line public protection services). Most provinces now *presume* that
   certain cancers in firefighters are work-related. How does a presumption change who gets counted?
4. Why might occupational cancer deaths be under-counted in other occupations?

# Part 7 (ENVH 460/560). Making rates

This dataset has no denominators. To compare provinces you need the number of workers covered by
each WCB (AWCBC publishes these in its Key Statistical Measures) or, as an approximation, the
number of employed people from Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey.

```{r rates}
# Employed people (thousands), 2024: replace these placeholders with figures from
# Statistics Canada table 14-10-0023-01 before interpreting the result
employment <- tibble(jurisdiction = c("ON", "QC", "BC", "AB"),
                     employed_thousands = c(NA_real_, NA_real_, NA_real_, NA_real_))

trend |>
  filter(outcome == "lost time claims", year == 2024) |>
  inner_join(employment, by = "jurisdiction") |>
  mutate(claims_per_100_workers = value / (employed_thousands * 1000) * 100)
```

**Questions**

1. Look up employment for these provinces and compute claims per 100 workers. Rank them.
2. Why is the number of employed people a poor denominator for workers' compensation claims?
   (Think about the self-employed and the share of workers covered by each WCB.)
3. Two provinces have similar rates. Can you conclude they are equally safe? List three reasons
   why not.

**Your answer:**
